--- title: "Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn" description: "Wildfires in Greece in official and satellite data: the area burnt each year since 1980, the worst years, the fire season, a map of every large fire since 2016, and the neighbours." author: "" date: "27 November 2026" --- ## What is this? In August 2023 a fire near Alexandroupolis burnt more than 96,000 hectares, the largest single fire in Europe since the 1980s ([JRC, 10 April 2024](https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/jrc-news-and-updates/wildfires-2023-among-worst-eu-century-2024-04-10_en)). A hectare is a square of 100 metres by 100; that fire burnt more than 960 square kilometres. Was it a sign that Greece burns more than it used to? This story asks five questions: 1. **Is Greece burning more than it used to?** 2. **Which were the worst years, and why?** 3. **Is the fire season getting longer?** 4. **Where do the fires burn?** 5. **How does Greece compare with its neighbours?** The data come from three places, besides the [boundaries of the regions](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/gisco/geodata/statistical-units/territorial-units-statistics) from GISCO and the area of each country from Eurostat ([reg_area3](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/reg_area3/default/table?lang=en)): - **National statistics:** the area burnt and the number of forest fires in each country, every year since 1980, which the countries report and the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission collects ([country totals](https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/applications/data-and-services)). Those of Greece count forest land, "wooded and non-wooded" ([JRC 2025](https://doi.org/10.2760/0649290)). - **EFFIS**, the European Forest Fire Information System, run by the JRC: satellites outline the land that burns. It has the area burnt in each country every year since 2006, in fires of about 30 hectares or more ([statistics portal](https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/apps/effis.statistics)), and the outline of every fire mapped in Greece since 2016, at first of about 30 hectares or more and, since 2020, smaller ones too ([rapid damage assessment](https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/about-effis/technical-background/rapid-damage-assessment)). - **NASA FIRMS**: the hot spots that two satellites, Terra and Aqua, have seen in Greece since 2003 ([FIRMS](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/tools/firms), with [one file for each country and year](https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/country/)). **They do not count the same things.** The national statistics count forest land; the satellites outline all the land that burnt, farmland included, but miss the small fires. In 2007, for example, Greece counted 225,734 hectares of forest fires, and another 88,093 in fires outside forest land, 313,826 in all ([JRC 2008](https://doi.org/10.2788/76413)); EFFIS mapped about 272,000 hectares, in fires of about 30 hectares or more. Where the two disagree, the page says which one it shows. --- ## Packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages(c("eurostat", "ggplot2", "ggrepel")) # install.packages(c("jsonlite", "plotly", "readxl", "sf")) library(eurostat) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(sf) ``` ::: ## The data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the country totals: an Excel file with one sheet for the area burnt (hectares) and one for the # number of fires, with a row for each year and a column for each country totals_file<-tempfile(fileext=".xlsx") download.file(paste0("https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/effis/applications/", "data-and-services/","report_2024.xlsx"), totals_file,mode="wb",quiet=TRUE) read_greece<-function(sheet) { x<-as.data.frame(readxl::read_excel(totals_file,sheet=sheet,col_types="text")) # numbers are written with spaces between the thousands, such as "32 965" result<-data.frame(year=as.integer(x$Year),value=as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.]","",x$GRC))) return(result) } national<-data.frame(year=read_greece(1)$year,area=read_greece(1)$value,fires=read_greece(2)$value) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # EFFIS's estimates for a country (its three-letter code): the area burnt each year, in hectares, # and the number of fires of about 30 hectares or more, from satellite images effis_annual<-function(code) { x<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0("https://api2.effis.emergency.copernicus.eu/statistics/v2/effis/", "estimatesbycountry?country=",code)) result<-data.frame(code=code,year=x$year,area=x$ba,fires=x$nf) return(result) } countries<-data.frame(code=c("GRC","PRT","ESP","ITA","FRA","CYP"), geo=c("EL","PT","ES","IT","FR","CY"), name=c("Greece","Portugal","Spain","Italy","France","Cyprus")) effis<-do.call(rbind,lapply(countries$code,effis_annual)) effis_greece<-effis[effis$code=="GRC",] # the area of each country, in square kilometres: for France, without its overseas departments area_all<-get_eurostat("reg_area3", filters=list(geo=c(countries$geo,"FRY"),landuse="TOTAL",unit="KM2"), time_format="num",cache=FALSE) area_now<-area_all[area_all$time==max(area_all$time),] land<-setNames(area_now$values,area_now$geo) countries$km2<-land[countries$geo]-ifelse(countries$geo=="FR",land["FRY"],0) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the outlines of the fires in Greece: EFFIS's map service, only those of the country EL wfs<-c(service="WFS",version="1.1.0",request="GetFeature",typename="ms:modis.ba.poly", outputformat="geojson", Filter=paste0("COUNTRY", "EL")) wfs_url<-paste0("https://maps.effis.emergency.copernicus.eu/effis?", paste0(names(wfs),"=",sapply(wfs,URLencode,reserved=TRUE),collapse="&")) fires<-st_make_valid(st_read(wfs_url,quiet=TRUE)) fires$date<-as.Date(substr(fires$FIREDATE,1,10)) fires$year<-as.integer(format(fires$date,"%Y")) fires$area<-as.numeric(fires$AREA_HA) last_fire<-max(fires$date) first_year<-min(fires$year) last_year<-max(fires$year) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the hot spots of one year: one file per country and year. Type 0 is a presumed vegetation fire, # and frp is the fire radiative power of the hot spot, in megawatts hot_spots_of<-function(year) { x<-read.csv(paste0("https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/data/country/modis/",year,"/modis_",year, "_Greece.csv")) result<-x[x$type==0,c("acq_date","frp")] return(result) } hot_spot_years<-2003:(as.integer(format(Sys.Date(),"%Y"))-1) hot_spots<-do.call(rbind,lapply(hot_spot_years,hot_spots_of)) hot_spots$date<-as.Date(hot_spots$acq_date) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the 13 regions of Greece (NUTS level 2), and the names of the smaller ones (level 3): EFFIS gives # the Greek name of the place of each fire, GISCO the name in Latin letters gisco<-"https://gisco-services.ec.europa.eu/distribution/v2/nuts/" regions<-st_read(paste0(gisco,"geojson/NUTS_RG_03M_2024_4326_LEVL_2.geojson"),quiet=TRUE) regions<-regions[regions$CNTR_CODE=="EL",] places<-read.csv(paste0(gisco,"csv/NUTS_AT_2024.csv"),encoding="UTF-8") places<-places[places$CNTR_CODE=="EL"&nchar(places$NUTS_ID)==5,] region_names<-c(EL30="Attica",EL41="North Aegean",EL42="South Aegean",EL43="Crete", EL51="East Macedonia and Thrace",EL52="Central Macedonia",EL53="West Macedonia", EL54="Epirus",EL61="Thessaly",EL62="Ionian Islands",EL63="West Greece", EL64="Central Greece",EL65="Peloponnese") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} red<-"#d62728" blue<-"#1f77b4" gray<-"#bdbdbd" dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the color of the notes # three periods of fires, from the earliest to the latest: one hue, from light to dark period_colors<-c("#fd8d3c","#d94801","#7f2704") # the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(), margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) { note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left", yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray)) result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"), yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),margin=margin, annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>% config(displaylogo=FALSE) return(result) } legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom") # a colour scale of steps for classes numbered 1, 2, ... (with zmin = 0.5): one colour for each # class color_steps<-function(colors) { n<-length(colors) result<-do.call(c, lapply(seq_len(n),function(i) list(list((i-1)/n,colors[i]),list(i/n,colors[i])))) return(result) } # numbers and dates in the text number<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE) return(result) } percent<-function(x,digits=0) { result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits),"%") return(result) } one<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1) return(result) } two<-function(x) { result<-format(round(x,2),nsmall=2) return(result) } and_list<-function(x) { if(length(x)<2) { return(paste(x)) } result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1)) return(result) } date_text<-function(d) { result<-paste(as.integer(format(d,"%d")),month.name[as.integer(format(d,"%m"))],format(d,"%Y")) return(result) } day_text<-function(j) { d<-as.Date(round(j)-1,origin="2001-01-01") result<-paste(as.integer(format(d,"%d")),month.name[as.integer(format(d,"%m"))]) return(result) } ``` ::: --- ## 1. Is Greece burning more than it used to? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} area_in<-function(year) { result<-national$area[national$year==year] return(result) } last_total<-max(national$year) worst<-head(national$year[order(-national$area)],5) decade_of<-function(year) { result<-ifelse(year>=2020,paste0("2020–",last_total),paste0(10*(year%/%10),"s")) return(result) } # each period: its years, the area burnt and the fires of an average year, and the size of a fire by_decade<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(national,decade_of(national$year)),function(x) { data.frame(decade=decade_of(x$year[1]), years=nrow(x), area_a_year=mean(x$area), fires_a_year=mean(x$fires), size_of_fire=sum(x$area)/sum(x$fires)) })) rownames(by_decade)<-NULL of_decade<-function(decade,column) { result<-by_decade[[column]][by_decade$decade==decade] return(result) } last_decade<-tail(by_decade$decade,1) # a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance of a pattern as strong as this without one trend_area<-cor.test(national$year,national$area,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value trend_fires<-cor.test(national$year,national$fires,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value # the area burnt by year, both sources side by side both<-merge(national,effis_greece,by="year",suffixes=c("_national","_effis")) ratio<-sum(both$area_effis)/sum(both$area_national) ``` ::: **Not steadily. The area burnt swings far more from one year to the next than it changes over the decades.** In the 45 years from 1980 to 2024, Greece's forest fires burnt between 3,517 hectares (2003) and 225,734 (2007). Five years, 1988, 2000, 2007, 2021 and 2023, make up 36% of everything that burnt in those 45 years. The averages of the decades differ less: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(by_decade[,c("decade","area_a_year","fires_a_year","size_of_fire")],digits=0, format.args=list(big.mark=","), col.names=c("Period","Hectares burnt a year","Fires a year","Hectares a fire")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Period | Hectares burnt a year| Fires a year| Hectares a fire| |:---------|---------------------:|------------:|---------------:| |1980s | 52,416| 1,264| 41| |1990s | 44,108| 1,748| 25| |2000s | 49,238| 1,694| 29| |2010s | 24,220| 946| 26| |2020–2024 | 60,262| 1,039| 58| ::: ::: A rank test finds no trend in the area burnt from year to year (a pattern as strong as this one would come up by chance 16 times in 100), but a fall in the number of fires (4 in 100). The average fire grew from 25 hectares in the 1990s to 58 in 2020–2024, which is because the number of fires fell while a few of them were enormous. The number needs care, though: since 1998 the Fire Service has been responsible for forest fires, instead of the Forest Service, and the two did not count in the same way ([European Commission 2001](https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/effis/reports-and-publications/annual-fire-reports/08-forest-fires-in-southern-europe-2000.pdf)). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bars<-national bars$worst<-bars$year%in%worst p<-plot_ly() %>% add_bars(data=bars[!bars$worst,],x=~year,y=~area/1000,name="Area burnt",marker=list(color=gray), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand haNational statistics") %>% add_bars(data=bars[bars$worst,],x=~year,y=~area/1000,name="The five worst years", marker=list(color=red), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand haNational statistics") # the average of each decade, as a line over its years for(k in seq_len(nrow(by_decade))) { years<-national$year[decade_of(national$year)==by_decade$decade[k]] p<-add_lines(p,x=c(min(years)-0.45,max(years)+0.45),y=rep(by_decade$area_a_year[k]/1000,2), name="Average of the period",legendgroup="average",showlegend=k==1, line=list(color="black",width=2.5), hovertemplate=paste0(by_decade$decade[k], ": %{y:.1f} thousand ha a year")) } p %>% add_markers(data=effis_greece,x=~year,y=~area/1000,name="Satellite maps (EFFIS)", marker=list(color=blue,size=8,line=list(color="white",width=1)), hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand haEFFIS") %>% chart("Area burnt by fires in Greece each year, thousand hectares", paste0("JRC, country totals (bars); EFFIS, fires of about 30 ha or more (dots). EFFIS's ", last_year,": to ",date_text(last_fire),"."), "Thousand hectares",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=110,b=90)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The 2010s were the quietest of the five periods, and the years from 2020 to 2024 the worst, 60,262 hectares a year, with two of the five worst years in them. But an average of five years says little when one of them burns 136,499 hectares and another 9,300. **The satellites agree, and go on to the present.** EFFIS maps more land than the national statistics count, farmland included: 13% more in the years that both have, and their highs and lows are the same ones. After the country totals end, it has 47,819 hectares for 2025 and 35,454 for 2026, up to 21 November 2026. For 2025 the national figure, still provisional, is 41,540 hectares of forest land in 561 fires ([JRC 2026](https://doi.org/10.2760/3888324)). --- ## 2. Which were the worst years, and why? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} largest<-st_drop_geometry(fires) largest<-head(largest[order(-largest$area),],10) place_english<-c(Evvoia="Evia","Kalymnos, Karpathos, Kasos, Kos, Rodos"="Rhodes and nearby islands", Ileia="Ilia","Dytiki Attiki"="West Attica", "Lakonia, Messinia"="Laconia and Messinia","Anatoliki Attiki"="East Attica", "Magnisia, Sporades"="Magnesia and the Sporades") latin<-places$NAME_LATN[match(largest$PROVINCE,places$NUTS_NAME)] largest$place<-ifelse(latin%in%names(place_english),place_english[latin],latin) ``` ::: **Years of heat, drought or wind, when a few fires became huge.** In the official record, the five worst years were: - **2007**, the worst year for forest fires ever recorded in Greece: 225,734 hectares of forest land. Three heatwaves in a row, with more than 46 °C in some places, a long drought and strong winds; at the end of August five fires in the Peloponnese burnt 170,000 hectares and two in Evia 25,000. 69 civilians, 9 seasonal firefighters and 2 pilots died ([JRC 2008](https://doi.org/10.2788/76413)). - **2000**: 145,033 hectares, nearly three times the average of the two decades before ([European Commission 2001](https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/effis/reports-and-publications/annual-fire-reports/08-forest-fires-in-southern-europe-2000.pdf)). - **2023**: 136,499 hectares, after the warmest July in 64 years and a heatwave from 12 to 26 July. In July there were fires in Attica, Rhodes, Evia, Corfu and near Volos, and from the middle of August in Evros and Rodopi. 23 civilians and one firefighter died ([JRC 2024](https://doi.org/10.2760/8027062)). - **1988**: 110,501 hectares. - **2021**: 108,418 hectares, in a summer that approached 46 °C, with the most notable heatwave, in length, for 35 years. Most of the large fires came between 3 and 11 August, among them those of Attica, Evia, Eastern Mani and Ancient Olympia ([JRC 2022](https://doi.org/10.2760/34094)). **The deadliest fire was not among the largest.** In July 2018 a fire of just over 1,000 hectares at Mati, in Attica, killed 100 people, in a year that was "relatively light" for the area burnt ([JRC 2019](https://doi.org/10.2760/1128)). The ten largest fires that EFFIS has outlined in Greece since 2016: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(data.frame(started=date_text(largest$date), place=largest$place, area=number(largest$area)), col.names=c("Started","Place","Area (hectares)"),align="llr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Started |Place | Area (hectares)| |:--------------|:-------------------------|---------------:| |19 August 2023 |Evros | 96,610| |3 August 2021 |Evia | 51,881| |18 July 2023 |Rhodes and nearby islands | 18,626| |4 August 2021 |Ilia | 18,400| |31 July 2026 |West Attica | 13,192| |17 July 2023 |West Attica | 11,662| |3 August 2021 |Laconia and Messinia | 11,209| |11 August 2024 |East Attica | 10,971| |16 August 2021 |West Attica | 10,175| |26 July 2023 |Magnesia and the Sporades | 8,634| ::: ::: These ten made up 46% of the area of all 1,794 fires outlined from 2016 to 2026; the fire near Alexandroupolis alone, in Evros, 18%. Most fires are small: 80% of the outlined fires were under 100 hectares, and they made up 5% of the area. **A year is bad because a few fires are huge, not because there are many.** --- ## 3. Is the fire season getting longer? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the heat that each day's fires gave off when the satellites passed, in megawatts: the sum of the # fire radiative power of the day's hot spots, and 0 on the days without hot spots heat_of_day<-tapply(hot_spots$frp,hot_spots$date,sum) all_days<-seq(as.Date(paste0(min(hot_spot_years),"-01-01")), as.Date(paste0(max(hot_spot_years),"-12-31")),by="day") daily<-data.frame(date=all_days,heat=as.vector(heat_of_day[as.character(all_days)])) daily$heat[is.na(daily$heat)]<-0 daily$year<-as.integer(format(daily$date,"%Y")) daily$day<-as.Date(paste0("2001-",format(daily$date,"%m-%d"))) # one calendar for every year big<-2000 # a big-fire day: the fires gave off 2,000 megawatts or more when the satellites passed big_days<-daily[daily$heat>=big,] big_days$j<-as.integer(format(big_days$date,"%j")) big_days$summer<-as.integer(format(big_days$date,"%m"))%in%6:9 # two periods of eleven years periods<-list("2003–2013"=2003:2013,"2015–2025"=2015:2025) period_numbers<-lapply(periods,function(years) { x<-big_days[big_days$year%in%years,] first<-tapply(x$j,x$year,min) last<-tapply(x$j,x$year,max) list(per_year=nrow(x)/length(years),outside=100*mean(!x$summer),first=median(first), last=median(last)) }) in_period<-function(k,what) { result<-period_numbers[[k]][[what]] return(result) } # the heat of a hot spot in each month (median of all years) spot_heat<-tapply(hot_spots$frp,format(hot_spots$date,"%b"),median) ``` ::: **Not that the satellites can see.** The chart shows every day since 2003, one row for each year and one square for each day. The colour is how much heat the fires of the day gave off when the satellites passed over, in megawatts: the sum of NASA's fire radiative power of all the hot spots of the day, the presumed vegetation fires only ([NASA's description of the hot spots](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/tools/firms/active-fire-data-attributes-modis-viirs)). The season of the big fires is the dark band of July and August. In the months around it there are many paler squares, especially in autumn, some of them probably farmers burning what is left in the fields: a hot spot gave off 10 megawatts in October and 46 in August (medians). The heat, not the number of hot spots, separates the big fires. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} heat_classes<-c("No fire seen","Under 200 MW","200 to 999 MW","1,000 to 1,999 MW", "2,000 MW or more") daily$class<-as.integer(cut(daily$heat,c(-Inf,0,200,1000,big,Inf))) month_starts<-as.Date(paste0("2001-",1:12,"-01")) # the days as a table: one row for each year, one column for each date (29 February has no date in # the calendar of 2001, and is left out) calendar<-daily[!is.na(daily$day),] calendar_days<-sort(unique(calendar$day)) calendar_years<-sort(unique(calendar$year)) cells<-cbind(match(calendar$year,calendar_years),match(calendar$day,calendar_days)) class_table<-matrix(NA,length(calendar_years),length(calendar_days)) class_table[cells]<-calendar$class heat_table<-matrix("",length(calendar_years),length(calendar_days)) heat_table[cells]<-paste(number(calendar$heat),"MW") plot_ly(x=calendar_days,y=calendar_years,z=class_table,type="heatmap",zmin=0.5,zmax=5.5, colorscale=color_steps(c("#f7f7f7","#fee6ce","#fdae6b","#e6550d","#7f2704")), text=heat_table, colorbar=list(orientation="h",x=0,xanchor="left",y=-0.08,yanchor="top",tickvals=1:5, ticktext=heat_classes,len=0.9,thickness=12,tickfont=list(size=9), tickangle=0)) %>% style(hovertemplate="%{x|%d %B} %{y}: %{text}") %>% chart("When Greece burns", paste0("NASA FIRMS, MODIS on Terra and Aqua, presumed vegetation fires. ", "Heat of the fires that the satellites saw, each day, megawatts."), x_axis=list(tickvals=month_starts+14,ticktext=month.abb,showgrid=FALSE), y_axis=list(tick0=2005,dtick=5,showgrid=FALSE),margin=list(t=60,b=130),note_y=-0.24) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: A big-fire day here is one on which the fires gave off 2,000 megawatts or more. In 2003–2013 there were 7.4 of them a year, in 2015–2025 8.2; 6% and 4% of them came outside the months from June to September. The first big-fire day of the year came on 29 June in 2003–2013 and 12 July in 2015–2025, and the last on 27 August and 5 September (medians of the years). Nothing in these numbers says that the season has become longer. That is not the last word. The authors of Greece's chapter in the JRC's report for 2025 write that climate change has "systematically extended the fire season" ([JRC 2026](https://doi.org/10.2760/3888324)), and hot days do come earlier and last later, at least in Athens, as [Athens Is Getting Hotter](ILLUSTRATION_ATHENS_HEAT.html) shows. But the hot spots show what did burn, not how much could have: in years without a spark in a dangerous week, or with firefighters who put a fire out in time, a longer dangerous season leaves no trace in them. There are other limits too: - **A hot spot is not a fire.** It is a square about a kilometre across in which the satellite saw heat ([NASA's frequently asked questions](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/tools/firms/faq)): a big fire makes many, and farm burning and other sources of heat make some too. - **The satellites see a fire only when they pass over, without cloud.** Their orbits have changed as well: since 2020 NASA has not been able to keep Terra's passing time from drifting earlier ([NASA](https://terra.nasa.gov/about/terra-orbital-drift-information)), so the two periods were not seen at exactly the same hours. - **23 years are few**, and the fires of a year depend on the weather of a few weeks. --- ## 4. Where do the fires burn? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fires_area<-st_transform(fires,3035) # an equal-area projection regions_area<-st_transform(st_make_valid(regions),3035) burnt<-st_union(st_geometry(fires_area)) # the land burnt at least once inside<-st_intersection(regions_area[,"NUTS_ID"],st_sf(geometry=burnt)) region_share<-data.frame(NUTS_ID=regions_area$NUTS_ID, land=as.numeric(st_area(regions_area))/1e4, burnt=as.numeric(st_area(inside))[match(regions_area$NUTS_ID, inside$NUTS_ID)]/1e4) region_share$share<-100*region_share$burnt/region_share$land region_share$name<-region_names[region_share$NUTS_ID] region_share<-region_share[order(region_share$share),] in_region<-function(id,column) { result<-region_share[[column]][region_share$NUTS_ID==id] return(result) } all_land<-sum(region_share$land) burnt_share<-100*sum(region_share$burnt)/all_land # what burnt: EFFIS gives, for each fire, the share of its area that was each kind of land cover<-c(BROADLEA="forest",CONIFER="forest",MIXED="forest",SCLEROPH="other natural land", TRANSIT="other natural land",OTHERNATLC="other natural land",AGRIAREAS="farmland", ARTIFSURF="other",OTHERLC="other") cover_share<-sapply(names(cover),function(column) { as.numeric(fires[[column]])/100*fires$area }) cover_share<-cover_share[!is.na(rowSums(cover_share)),] cover_total<-tapply(colSums(cover_share),cover,sum) cover_percent<-100*cover_total/sum(cover_total) ``` ::: **Attica the most for its size, then the north-east and the Aegean.** By 21 November 2026, EFFIS had outlined 1,794 fires in Greece since 2016. EFFIS gets these shares by laying the outlines on the EU's CORINE map of land cover ([EFFIS, fire damage assessment](https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/about-effis/technical-background/fire-damage-assessment)). --- ## 5. How does Greece compare with its neighbours? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} compare<-effis[effis$year%in%2006:2025,] compare<-merge(compare,countries[,c("code","name","km2")]) # 1% of a square kilometre is one hectare, so hectares per square kilometre are a percentage compare$share<-compare$area/compare$km2 # each country: the share burnt in an average year, and its worst year, from the lowest average means<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(compare,compare$name),function(x) { data.frame(name=x$name[1], mean=mean(x$share), worst=max(x$share), worst_year=x$year[which.max(x$share)]) })) means<-means[order(means$mean),] rownames(means)<-NULL in_country<-function(name,column) { result<-means[[column]][means$name==name] return(result) } # the country with the highest share of each year top_of_year<-compare[compare$share==ave(compare$share,compare$year,FUN=max),] first_place<-table(top_of_year$name) times_first<-function(name) { result<-if(name%in%names(first_place)) first_place[[name]] else 0 return(result) } ``` ::: **Portugal burns the most for its size, and Greece is second.** In the years from 2006 to 2025, the satellites found that fires burnt on average 1.14% of Portugal every year and 0.38% of Greece: 3.0 times as much. Greece was ahead of Cyprus (0.26%), Spain (0.19%), Italy (0.19%) and France (0.03%). In 3 of the 20 years Greece had the highest share of all six, in 16 Portugal. Here EFFIS's satellites measure all six countries in the same way, in fires of about 30 hectares or more, so the comparison does not depend on how each country counts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) compare$position<-match(compare$name,means$name)+runif(nrow(compare),-0.17,0.17) # the worst year of each country, beside its row worst_labels<-lapply(seq_len(nrow(means)),function(i) { list(x=means$worst[i],y=i,text=paste0(means$worst_year[i]),showarrow=FALSE,xanchor="left", xshift=8,font=list(size=12,color=dark_gray)) }) plot_ly() %>% add_markers(data=compare,x=~share,y=~position, marker=list(color=ifelse(compare$name=="Greece",red,gray),size=9, line=list(color="white",width=1)), text=~paste0(name," ",year,": ",two(share),"%"), hovertemplate="%{text}",showlegend=FALSE) %>% add_markers(data=means,x=~mean,y=~match(name,means$name), marker=list(color=ifelse(means$name=="Greece",red,dark_gray),symbol="line-ns-open", size=26,line=list(width=4)), text=~paste0(name,", average 2006–2025: ",two(mean),"% a year"), hovertemplate="%{text}",showlegend=FALSE) %>% chart("Land burnt each year, % of the country, 2006–2025", paste0("EFFIS, fires of about 30 ha or more; areas of the countries: Eurostat, reg_area3. ", "Dots: years. Bars: averages."), x_axis=list(rangemode="tozero",ticksuffix="%"), y_axis=list(tickvals=seq_len(nrow(means)),ticktext=means$name,range=c(0.4,nrow(means)+0.6), zeroline=FALSE), annotations=worst_labels,margin=list(l=80,t=70,b=90,r=40),note_y=-0.14) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The number beside each country's row marks its worst year: 2017 in Portugal, 2007 in Greece, 2025 in Cyprus. --- ## So, what does it mean? 1. **Greece does not burn steadily more, but it burns in bursts.** Five years, 1988, 2000, 2007, 2021 and 2023, have 36% of everything that burnt from 1980 to 2024, and there is no trend in the total. 2. **A bad year is made of a few enormous fires.** The ten largest fires made up 46% of the area of the 1,794 fires outlined since 2016. 3. **The satellites see no longer season of big fires**, though the heat that makes a fire dangerous does last longer, and the Greek authors of the JRC's report say that the season has. 4. **Attica burns the most for its size**: more than a fifth of its land burnt at least once since 2016. 5. **Greece is second to Portugal.** Every year it burns about 0.38% of its land on average, against 0.19% in Spain and 0.19% in Italy. **What this does not show.** It does not say what started the fires, how well they were fought, or what the climate will do to the next ones. The national statistics and the satellites do not count the same things, the satellites miss the small fires, and the outlines show where a fire burnt, not how severely. And the fires are counted in hectares here, which do not measure the people, the homes and the animals lost in them.
